identification.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) as a North Korea-linked threat actor and says it has tracked the actor since 2020 and that its phishing operations have grown significantly more sophisticated over the past several years [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports it compromising aerospace and defense-related organizations, signing malware with legitimate but compromised certificates taken from victims, and distributing backdoored VPN clients and other legitimate software [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S2]. The Microsoft naming mapping used by this encyclopedia also lists VELVET CHOLLIMA as an alias [S8]. NAMING CONFLICT: several secondary sources and vendors list Ruby Sleet as an alias of APT37/ScarCruft (also InkySquid, Reaper, Ricochet Chollima, RedEyes) [S5][S6], while CrowdStrike's Velvet Chollima profile is the name usually associated with Kimsuky-related activity and lists Cerium and Ruby Sleet among community identifiers [S9]. Cluster boundaries across Microsoft, MITRE and CrowdStrike are not reconciled here; facts below are attributed only to the vendor that stated them. The 2023-2024 Microsoft reports cited do not themselves state a mapping to APT37 or Kimsuky [S1][S2].

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK). Microsoft's September 2023 East Asia report groups Ruby Sleet with other North Korean actors and says the North Korean government appears to assign multiple threat actor groups at once to meet high-priority collection requirements [S2]. Malpedia describes it as linked to North Korea's Ministry of State Security [S7]; that is a third-party catalog statement, not a Microsoft or government finding.
attribution.confidence: No explicit Microsoft confidence statement for Ruby Sleet was found in the sources reviewed [S1][S2]. No government attribution located.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident observation (victim compromises, supply-chain incident, infrastructure) [S1][S2]; Microsoft's interpretation of overlapping targeting across North Korean actors [S2].

objectives: Collection of defense, aerospace and maritime-sector information. Microsoft says stolen aerospace and defense technology may be used by North Korea to increase its understanding of missiles, drones and related technologies [S1]. Microsoft assessed the 2022-2023 maritime and shipbuilding targeting as occurring shortly before North Korean maritime military tests in March and April 2023, which included underwater attack drones [S2].

sectors: Construction (Korean company used as a supply-chain entry point)
regions: Russia (aerospace research institute, March 2023, with Onyx Sleet) [S2]
Germany and Israel (two arms manufacturing companies, with Diamond Sleet, November 2022 to January 2023) [S2]
targeting.notes: Maritime and shipbuilding targeting November 2022 to January 2023 was conducted alongside Diamond Sleet and Sapphire Sleet [S2][S3]. Microsoft's regions beyond those listed are not stated in the sources reviewed.

capabilities.summary: Social-engineering and phishing operations that Microsoft says have become significantly more sophisticated; reconnaissance to identify the software a target uses and custom capabilities built for specific targets; malware signed with legitimate but compromised certificates obtained from victims; distribution of backdoored VPN clients, installers and other legitimate software [S1]. In December 2023 Microsoft observed the actor compromise a Korean construction company and replace a legitimate Wizvera VeraPort software version with one that communicated with known Ruby Sleet infrastructure [S1]. No named malware families are given in the Microsoft sources reviewed [S1][S2]. If Ruby Sleet is treated as APT37, Zscaler's 2026 reporting on the 'Ruby Jumper' campaign describes RESTLEAF (Zoho WorkDrive C2), SNAKEDROPPER, THUMBSBD (USB-based air-gap bridging), VIRUSTASK and FOOTWINE [S4]; that mapping is a secondary-source alias claim and not confirmed by Microsoft here [S5].

campaigns.name: Ruby Jumper (APT37-attributed by Zscaler; mapping to Ruby Sleet via alias lists only)
campaigns.summary: Zscaler ThreatLabz reported an APT37 campaign using malicious LNK files and Zoho WorkDrive C2 to reach air-gapped systems via USB. Linking it to Ruby Sleet depends on third-party alias lists, not on a Microsoft statement.

diamond.adversary: North Korea-linked actor tracked by Microsoft as Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S1][S2]. Third parties variously equate it with APT37/ScarCruft or place it near Kimsuky-associated names; unresolved [S5][S9].
diamond.capability: Phishing, stolen-certificate code signing, backdoored VPN clients and installers, and software supply-chain replacement (VeraPort) [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Microsoft refers to 'known Ruby Sleet infrastructure' contacted by the trojanized VeraPort package; specifics are not published in the sources reviewed [S1]. Compromised victim certificates serve as signing infrastructure [S1].
diamond.victim: Aerospace and defense organizations, maritime and shipbuilding firms, arms manufacturers in Germany and Israel, a Russian aerospace research institute, and a Korean construction company [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting North Korean missile, drone and maritime-military development, as assessed by Microsoft [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Software trust relationships (VPN clients, VeraPort-style identity/plug-in delivery, code-signing certificates) and defense-contractor email and software supply chains [S1].

gaps: Cluster mapping is unresolved: sources equate Ruby Sleet with APT37/ScarCruft [S5][S6], CrowdStrike lists Cerium and Ruby Sleet as community identifiers under Velvet Chollima [S9], and the Microsoft reports cited do not state a mapping. The Microsoft naming mapping file was retrieved by the encyclopedia but its entry text was not re-verified here [S8].

Whether Zscaler's Ruby Jumper campaign (2025-2026) belongs to Microsoft's Ruby Sleet cluster is unverified; Zscaler's own blog could not be opened (host blocked) and it was read only through secondary coverage [S4].
Malpedia's Ministry of State Security statement was read only through search results and its basis is not given [S7].
No named malware families, hashes, domains or IP indicators for Ruby Sleet are published in the Microsoft sources reviewed.
Microsoft's CYBERWARCON article gives no explicit confidence level or victim count; the December 2023 construction-company incident rests on that single source [S1].
Microsoft's September 2023 full report PDF and the Register article were read via summary and search snippets, not in full [S2][S3].
No US government (CISA, FBI, DOJ, Treasury) attribution or advisory specific to Ruby Sleet was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes defense-industrial-base and aerospace email, VPN client distribution channels, code-signing certificate stores, and software update or plug-in delivery channels (e.g. VeraPort-style) used by contractors and their suppliers [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is assessed by Microsoft as seeking missile, drone and maritime-related technology, and has coordinated with other North Korean actors against the same sector [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is targeted phishing and reconnaissance, then trojanized legitimate software or backdoored VPN clients signed with stolen certificates, then collection from aerospace, defense and shipbuilding victims [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against allied and non-allied aerospace, defense and maritime firms, including through supplier compromise. MDCOA is use of a compromised supplier's signed software to reach defense contractors at scale during a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected updates to VPN clients or identity plug-ins, validly signed binaries from unusual publishers or recently compromised vendors, and beaconing from newly installed client software [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft and vendor reporting on North Korean clusters together, since Microsoft observed multiple groups on the same targets and naming across vendors does not align [S2][S9]. (2) Authorities and coordination: supply-chain incidents at contractors are best routed through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels with the affected company and, for foreign partners, through established allied intelligence-sharing arrangements. (3) Mission assurance: verify code-signing trust, third-party VPN client provenance and software-update integrity for mission-relevant systems; treat valid signatures as insufficient evidence of legitimacy [S1]. (4) Avoid attributing incidents to Ruby Sleet by alias alone until the cluster mapping is resolved.
